edition.deck: Evacuations from occupied Ukraine, a major crypto theft and new pressure on election officials lead this morning’s briefing.
edition.editorialNote: The morning agenda prioritises overnight developments and consequential continuing stories. Danish coverage favours fresh reporting, including new legal and investigative angles, over stories repeated unchanged from the previous edition.

content.headline: Hundreds leave Russian-occupied Oleshky as residents describe desperate hardship
content.shortHeadline: Oleshky evacuees describe life under occupation
content.standfirst: A ceasefire window has allowed residents to leave the front-line city, where some say they faced hunger, minefields and attacks. Many people remain, and the truce is due to end on Sunday.

image.caption: Oleshky evacuees reunite with loved ones after leaving the occupied city.

sources.originalTitle: 'We came back from hell', say Ukrainians after years in Russia-occupied front-line city
De har spist ukrudt for at overleve – nu evakueres indbyggere fra "helvede på jord"

segments.body: Hundreds of residents have been evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky and crossed into northern Ukraine via Belarus. Olha and Viacheslav, who left with their family, told the BBC that they had struggled to find food as shelling intensified and escape routes remained dangerous.

segments.title: Those still there
segments.body: A separate account describes families surviving on small food supplies, sometimes including garden weeds. Supplies were also taken into the city during the evacuation. Hundreds are reported to have stayed behind; it remains unclear how many people left, and the ceasefire is expected to expire on Sunday.

content.headline: Binance says it has covered 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
content.shortHeadline: Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
content.standfirst: The FBI says North Korea was responsible for the theft from the cryptocurrency exchange. Binance says it will cover the remaining losses, while the investigation continues and withdrawals are expected to resume on Sunday.

sources.originalTitle: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
Binance says 90% of losses from $6.3bn hack covered as FBI says North Korea behind attack

segments.body: Binance says it has replaced 90% of the $6.3bn in assets stolen in what it believes is the largest crypto hack on record. The FBI attributes the theft to North Korea; the remaining assets may take longer to source, the exchange says. Binance says customers will not bear the financial loss.

segments.title: Recovery and investigation
segments.body: Binance says it used company funds and reserves to replace the assets and is on track to resume withdrawals on Sunday, though it has yet to confirm the details. The investigation is ongoing. The FBI says the attackers are converting stolen assets and has urged companies to block transactions linked to addresses used in the laundering.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that bitcoin, Ethereum and Binance’s BNB token fell after the theft was announced. It also details how Binance drew on its user-protection fund, futures insurance fund and corporate treasury to replenish assets.

content.headline: US judge orders Trump administration to stop threatening election officials
content.shortHeadline: Judge bars threats against US election officials
content.standfirst: A federal judge says the administration’s demands to set aside ballots could interfere with election administration and disenfranchise eligible voters. The ruling comes days before the midterm elections.

sources.originalTitle: Judge orders Trump administration to stop threatening US election officials

segments.body: A federal judge in California has ordered the US government to stop threatening local and state election officials with criminal charges over ballot processing. The order also bars the Justice Department from demanding that officials set aside ballots it alleges may have been cast by non-citizens.

segments.title: The dispute over ballots
segments.body: The ruling follows letters demanding that officials set aside ballots belonging to 20,000 registered voters in California and similar demands in Washington state. The administration says it is pursuing unlawful voting; the judge said its actions were likely to interfere with election administration and disenfranchise lawful voters. Research cited by the BBC indicates that convictions of non-citizens for voting are rare.

content.headline: Russia’s Novaya Gazeta says it has been forced to close
content.shortHeadline: Novaya Gazeta says Kremlin pressure forced closure
content.standfirst: The independent newspaper says Russian authorities blocked its website and banned its print edition, making it impossible to operate. Former editor Dmitry Muratov blames the Kremlin; the newspaper’s closure marks a sharp new blow to independent reporting.

image.caption: Former editor Dmitry Muratov with a copy of Novaya Gazeta.

source.credit: Foto: David Dee Delgado / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Dræbte journalister og Nobels Fredspris – nu er Ruslands sidste frie avis "kvalt"

segments.body: Novaya Gazeta says it is stopping publication after Russian authorities blocked its website and banned its print edition. Former editor Dmitry Muratov told the BBC that restrictions made it impossible for the newspaper to earn money, including by preventing banks from accepting readers’ donations.

segments.title: A long squeeze
segments.body: The newspaper’s staff and output in Russia had already shrunk since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Its current editor says the authorities forced the editorial team to stop working. Several of the paper’s journalists have been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot in 2006.

content.headline: Cost-of-living protests turn violent in France and Germany
content.shortHeadline: Cost-of-living protests turn violent in France and Germany
content.standfirst: Large demonstrations over living costs and public services were mostly peaceful before clashes and looting broke out in several cities. Organisers in Germany cited concerns including school funding, public spending and compulsory military service.

image.caption: A protester uses a firework during a demonstration in France.

sources.originalTitle: Police clash with masked rioters after largely peaceful protests across France
Shops looted as German cost of living protests turn violent

segments.body: In France, about 320,000 people joined demonstrations on Saturday, according to the interior ministry. Clashes followed in Paris, Marseille and other cities as masked groups fought police; authorities said 565 people were arrested nationwide. Organisers included students, trade unions and yellow-vest protesters.

segments.title: Unrest in Germany
segments.body: In Germany, thousands also marched over the cost of living and public services. Police reported violence in Frankfurt, Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, including smashed shop windows and attacks on emergency workers. The German demonstrations were organised by Gen Z regelt, a campaign group whose spokesperson said it opposed compulsory military service.

perspectives.body: The BBC reports that authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin estimated up to 18,000 protesters, around half the number organisers had expected. Frankfurt police said weapons were seized after a suspect was arrested.

content.headline: Ebola outbreak in DR Congo passes 5,000 deaths
content.shortHeadline: Ebola deaths pass 5,000 in DR Congo outbreak
content.standfirst: More than 10,300 cases have been confirmed across eight provinces in the country’s deadliest recorded outbreak. Conflict, attacks on health workers and the absence of a vaccine for this strain are complicating efforts to contain it.

image.caption: Clinical trials are under way, but there is no vaccine for the strain causing the outbreak.

sources.originalTitle: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak

segments.body: More than 5,000 people have died in the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with over 10,300 confirmed cases across eight provinces, government data shows. The outbreak began in May and became the country’s deadliest on record in August.

segments.title: Difficult to contain
segments.body: The epicentre is in Ituri, a conflict zone, and attacks on health workers have added to the difficulties of containing the virus. Testing, treatment and vaccine trials are under way, but there is not yet a vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain responsible for this outbreak. Two suspected cases in Nigeria were being tested on Saturday, the report said.

content.headline: Poland’s constitutional court dispute deepens as protests follow shake-up
content.shortHeadline: Poland’s court crisis deepens as protests continue
content.standfirst: Prime Minister Donald Tusk says his government must restore a court he says was undermined by the previous administration. The opposition and human-rights groups dispute the legality of the latest move, and protests have followed.

image.caption: Police face demonstrators outside Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal.

sources.originalTitle: Tusk defends overhaul of Poland’s constitutional court despite protests
Tre anholdt og hundredvis på gaden i Polen efter suspendering af præsident for domstol

segments.body: Poland’s constitutional court crisis has intensified after government-backed judges moved to take procedural control of the tribunal and suspend its chief judge and deputy. Protesters gathered outside the court; police said three people were arrested after demonstrators forced a security barrier.

segments.title: A disputed legal path
segments.body: Tusk says the changes are needed to restore the rule of law after years of political disputes over the court. The Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights questioned the legal basis for the temporary suspension, while President Karol Nawrocki and opposition figures accuse the government of unlawfully taking over a constitutional institution. The legality remains disputed.

content.headline: India’s opposition plans rally over voter-roll changes affecting millions
content.shortHeadline: India opposition to rally over voter-roll changes
content.standfirst: The Congress party expects a major demonstration in Delhi against a voter-list revision that has removed 130 million names from draft rolls. The Election Commission says the exercise updates the register; opposition parties fear eligible voters could be excluded.

image.caption: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has urged supporters to attend the Delhi rally.

sources.originalTitle: India's opposition set to hold mega rally seeking election chief's resignation

segments.body: India’s main opposition Congress party plans to hold a large rally in Delhi on Sunday, calling for the chief election commissioner to resign and for electoral reforms. The protest comes amid controversy over a voter-roll revision that has removed 130 million names from draft lists across the country.

segments.title: Competing claims
segments.body: The Election Commission says the revision removes people who have died or moved away. Opposition parties allege that eligible voters could be left off the rolls and that the changes could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s party; both the commission and the governing BJP deny wrongdoing. Police have imposed conditions on the rally and deployed thousands of security personnel.

content.headline: MoD officials say UK police should have retained case against US pilot
content.shortHeadline: MoD officials say UK should have kept US pilot case
content.standfirst: Documents show defence officials privately judged that police should not have handed a case involving a US airman to the military. The disclosure adds to a government inquiry into how serious crimes by US personnel in Britain are handled.

image.caption: Jacob Wulfson’s case was heard at a US court martial on an airbase in England.

sources.originalTitle: UK police should not have let US force take over airbase trial, MoD documents show
‘Degrading’: why did a US fighter pilot avoid British trial after strangling a woman in England?

segments.body: Ministry of Defence officials said Cambridgeshire police should not have handed the investigation of US pilot Jacob Wulfson to US military police, according to documents obtained by the Guardian. Wulfson was tried by a US court martial after an assault on Sarah Steele in Cambridge while he was off duty.

segments.title: Who has jurisdiction?
segments.body: Under a long-standing UK-US agreement, British police have the primary right to investigate alleged crimes by US personnel, with exceptions for offences committed on duty or against military personnel or property. MoD officials said the Steele case did not appear to meet those exceptions. A cross-government inquiry is examining other cases in which British police handed investigations to US military authorities.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s earlier account details how Steele testified at the court martial and described the process as degrading. Wulfson was convicted of strangulation but acquitted of sexual assault, and received a six-month sentence.

content.headline: Almost 140 arrested at London protest against Palestine Action ban
content.shortHeadline: 139 arrested at protest against Palestine Action ban
content.standfirst: Police arrested 139 people at a protest outside the US embassy against the group’s proscription. The Metropolitan police said demonstrators intended to commit an offence; the protest organisers dispute the police response. An appeal is due this week.

image.caption: Police remove a demonstrator at a protest outside the US embassy in London.

sources.originalTitle: Almost 140 arrested at protest against Palestine Action ban outside US embassy in London

segments.body: The Metropolitan police said 139 people were arrested at a demonstration outside the US embassy in London opposing the proscription of Palestine Action. Protesters held signs expressing support for the group; police said that supporting a proscribed organisation was unlawful.

segments.title: Appeal ahead
segments.body: The demonstration was organised by Defend Our Juries, which said about 400 people attended and accused police of overreacting. The protest took place before a Supreme Court appeal against the proscription, scheduled for 4 November. The police said officers remained at the scene and continued making arrests.

content.headline: Care worker says home secretary barred him from meeting over settlement plans
content.shortHeadline: Care worker says home secretary barred him from meeting
content.standfirst: A Nigerian care worker says he was left in tears after the Home Secretary’s office excluded him from a union meeting. The dispute comes as the government considers proposals that could extend some migrants’ wait for settlement to 15 years.

image.caption: Care worker Kolade says he felt humiliated after being excluded from the meeting.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Was I not enough?’: care worker barred from meeting home secretary

segments.body: Kolade, a care worker chosen by fellow migrant workers to represent them, says the Home Secretary’s office told his union he could not attend a scheduled meeting with Shabana Mahmood. Unison says the reason given was that his presence was “inappropriate”; Kolade says the decision left him feeling humiliated.

segments.title: Proposed settlement changes
segments.body: The meeting was due to discuss earned-settlement proposals that could lengthen the standard qualifying period from five to 10 years, with some lower-paid workers facing 15 years. The Home Office said it was considering more than 200,000 consultation responses and that it would not have been appropriate to prioritise one person’s views. Unison says ministers should hear directly from care workers.

content.headline: UK government plans to ringfence spending on prevention
content.shortHeadline: UK to protect some spending aimed at preventing future costs
content.standfirst: A new budget rule is intended to protect programmes judged to save money or prevent problems over time. Its scope is not yet defined, leaving open questions about what qualifies and how departments will argue for protected funds.

image.caption: John Healey and Andy Burnham in the Commons after the budget.

sources.originalTitle: A world-first focus on long-term outcomes could transform UK government – or create new spending fights

segments.body: From the next spending review, the government plans to ringfence some preventative spending through a new budget category. The aim is to stop programmes expected to reduce future costs being raided to meet more immediate demands. The budget identifies spending to prevent rough sleeping as one possible example.

segments.title: The definition is still open
segments.body: Departments are waiting for Treasury guidance on what will qualify. The Institute for Government’s Stuart Hoddinott said the definition matters because almost any spending could be argued to prevent future costs. Officials also warn that the new rule could create fresh disputes between departments and the Treasury over which programmes deserve protection.

content.headline: RAF drone tracks Russian ships in first operational Channel mission
content.shortHeadline: RAF drone tracks Russian ships in first Channel mission
content.standfirst: The unarmed Protector RG1 spent more than 10 hours monitoring Russian vessels, in the first operational RAF drone deployment in the English Channel, the Ministry of Defence says. The mission adds surveillance capacity, but does not resolve wider strain on the Navy.

image.caption: An RAF Protector RG1 drone used to monitor Russian naval activity.

sources.originalTitle: The images that show the UK’s new tactic to trail Russian ships in the Channel

segments.body: An RAF Protector RG1 drone flew over the English Channel for more than 10 hours to monitor Russian vessels, working alongside Royal Navy ships and helicopters. The Ministry of Defence says this was the first operational deployment of an RAF remotely piloted aircraft in the Channel.

segments.title: A longer watch
segments.body: The operation, conducted between late September and mid-October, also covered Russian activity in the North Sea and waters west of Scotland. Defence analyst Sam Cranny-Evans said a drone able to remain on station for hours could provide surveillance at lower cost than crewed aircraft. He cautioned that it does not address the Navy’s wider shortages of personnel, ships and funding.

content.headline: Gordon Brown’s influence reported in UK defence-finance decision
content.shortHeadline: Brown’s role in UK defence-finance plans comes under scrutiny
content.standfirst: The i Paper reports that Gordon Brown helped steer the government away from a Canadian-led defence bank and towards a separate UK-backed plan. Sources disagree over the decision-making and its effect on relations with Canada.

image.caption: Former prime minister Gordon Brown is a political mentor to Chancellor John Healey.

sources.originalTitle: Gordon Brown’s hidden influence over Burnham’s Budget

segments.body: The UK is pursuing a Treasury-backed mechanism with other NATO members to finance additional defence spending, rather than joining a Canadian-led defence bank. The i Paper reports that former prime minister Gordon Brown argued for the alternative, while Treasury sources say Chancellor John Healey made the final decision.

segments.title: Two approaches
segments.body: The Canadian-led bank aims to make defence financing more accessible to governments and companies. The UK-backed plan is designed to coordinate and finance joint arms purchases. Sources cited by the paper say the split has caused friction; the Treasury and Canada’s finance department said the two institutions could work in partnership.

content.headline: Online resale competition adds to pressure on UK charity shops
content.shortHeadline: Charity shops face pressure as online resale grows
content.standfirst: Accounts reported by the Financial Times show Oxfam’s retail profit fell 23%, while other charities have closed or plan to close stores. Some sector figures point to online resale; others cite staffing costs and the declining quality of donations.

image.caption: An Oxfam charity shop in London.

sources.originalTitle: UK charity shop profits plummet amid shift in secondhand clothes market

segments.body: Oxfam’s retail profit fell 23% to £4.9m in the last financial year, according to accounts seen by the Financial Times. The British Heart Foundation plans to close 150 shops after its stores recorded a loss, while Cancer Research UK and Scope have also closed or are closing some locations.

segments.title: More than one pressure
segments.body: The shift comes as secondhand clothing sales have grown and platforms such as Vinted and Depop connect sellers directly with buyers. The Charity Retail Association says online resale is not a major problem for its members and points instead to rising costs, including higher National Insurance. Charity leaders also stress that shops provide community links and volunteer opportunities as well as income.

content.headline: Medical micro-robots move closer to targeted drug delivery
content.shortHeadline: Micro-robots show promise for targeted drug delivery
content.standfirst: Researchers are developing tiny devices that could deliver drugs to precise sites in the body. Some capsule-based cameras are already used in NHS investigations, but robots designed to treat disease remain experimental.

image.caption: Illustration of a micro-robot designed to deliver drugs inside the gut.

sources.originalTitle: The astonishing micro-robots you swallow that spot cancer and might help treat it

segments.body: A swallowable camera capsule is already used to investigate gut problems, and newer systems can be steered around the stomach using magnets. Researchers are developing smaller devices that could deliver medicines to specific sites, potentially reducing the dose needed to have an effect.

segments.title: Still experimental
segments.body: Researchers in Beijing reported using a 6.5mm device to deliver insulin to the lower intestine of pigs. Separately, a Swiss team demonstrated a 2mm robot guided through a pig’s bloodstream. These are research-stage developments; the report says devices small enough to travel through blood vessels are likely at least a decade away from use in patients.

content.headline: Denmark seeks $22m from US company over alleged tax-fraud proceeds
content.shortHeadline: Denmark seeks $22m over alleged tax-fraud proceeds
content.standfirst: Danish authorities allege that an Arizona property company received money linked to the dividend-tax fraud case and used it to buy property. The company denies knowingly handling fraud proceeds; the case in Dubai has not been decided.

image.caption: Cigarette packages marketed on Emerald’s website.

sources.originalTitle: Afsløring: Dansk milliardjagt fører til mystisk amerikansk cigaretfirma

segments.body: Danish authorities allege that US company Emerald Industries received money linked to the dividend-tax fraud case involving Sanjay Shah and used it to buy Arizona property. Denmark is seeking control of the properties or compensation of more than $22m in proceedings in Dubai.

segments.title: The allegation is disputed
segments.body: Emerald denies knowingly receiving or handling proceeds of fraud and says payments related to legitimate cigarette sales. The company has also argued the case should not be heard in Dubai. The court rejected its attempt to have the case dismissed, but it has not ruled on whether the money came from the fraud or whether Denmark will recover the assets.

content.headline: Biodiversity deal reached at COP17, but Denmark has not filed its targets
content.shortHeadline: Global biodiversity deal reached as Denmark misses reporting
content.standfirst: Countries agreed steps to protect nature at the UN summit in Armenia, but funding remains unresolved. Denmark attended without submitting the national targets and progress report required under the biodiversity framework.

image.caption: Delegates at COP17 after reaching a biodiversity agreement.

sources.originalTitle: COP17-aftale skal genoprette klodens natur - men pengene mangler

segments.body: Countries at the UN biodiversity summit in Armenia agreed to reduce subsidies that harm nature and increase financial support for developing countries. They also acknowledged that progress towards global nature targets is too slow, but the agreement leaves funding unclear.

segments.title: Denmark’s missing report
segments.body: Denmark took part without submitting the national biodiversity targets or progress report required under the Kunming-Montreal framework. The report says nine out of 10 countries have set targets. Denmark was represented by officials, while its minister for nature and animal welfare did not attend.

content.headline: Trump shares image portraying Greenland as a US military base
content.shortHeadline: Trump shares image of Greenland as US military base
content.standfirst: The image shows a runway, military aircraft and a US flag, with the caption “Welcome to Greenland”. It is the latest in a series of altered Greenland images shared by the president; the purpose of the posts is unclear.

image.caption: Image shared by Donald Trump depicting Greenland as a US military base.

sources.originalTitle: Én stor militærbase: Trump deler nyt billede af Grønland

segments.body: Donald Trump shared an image on Truth Social depicting Greenland as a US military base, with a long runway, military aircraft and an American flag. He posted it with the words “Welcome to Greenland” and no further explanation.

segments.title: A repeated theme
segments.body: The post follows earlier altered images of Greenland shared by Trump, including one that placed the US flag over Greenland and Iceland. Denmark, Greenland and the United States agreed in September that the US would build two military bases on the island. The purpose of the latest post remains unclear.

content.headline: Danish culture minister and entrepreneur clash in televised AI debate
content.shortHeadline: Danish minister and entrepreneur clash in AI debate
content.standfirst: Zenia Stampe says she regrets directing her anger at entrepreneur Martin Thorborg during a heated discussion about artificial intelligence. Both participants say they were upset by the exchange, which has prompted criticism of the debate’s tone.

image.caption: Zenia Stampe and Martin Thorborg during their televised debate about AI.

source.credit: Foto: / Niels Ahlmann Olesen/Berlingske/Ritzau Scanpix & Asger Ladefoged/Berlingske/Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Minister mødt af massiv kritik efter tv-program: - Jeg var bange for at se det

segments.body: Culture Minister Zenia Stampe and entrepreneur Martin Thorborg repeatedly interrupted one another during a televised discussion about AI and his AI-assisted autobiography. Stampe later said she wished she had directed her anger at what he represented rather than at him personally.

segments.title: Different accounts of the exchange
segments.body: Thorborg said he was shaken and felt Stampe criticised a book she had not read, while acknowledging that he also used sharp language. A conflict mediator interviewed by TV 2 said there were signs that the discussion was becoming personal and that participants shared responsibility for bringing it back to the subject.

content.headline: TV 2 could face legal complaint over hidden-camera show, lecturer says
content.shortHeadline: Lecturer says TV 2 may face legal complaint over hidden cameras
content.standfirst: A media studies lecturer says filming in private settings without consent could breach Denmark’s criminal code. Rasmus Wallbridge has not said whether he will withdraw his consent, and no court has ruled on the matter.

image.caption: Rasmus Wallbridge in TV 2’s hidden-camera series Alle elsker Rasmus.

sources.originalTitle: Lektor: Wallbridge kan melde TV 2 for brud på straffeloven
TV 2 fjerner 'Alle Elsker Rasmus' efter massiv kritik
Komiker Rasmus Wallbridge bryder tavsheden med Instagram-opslag

segments.body: Media studies lecturer Thomas Pallesen says TV 2 may have breached a law against photographing people in private settings without permission while making the hidden-camera series Alle elsker Rasmus. He says comedian Rasmus Wallbridge could bring a case if he withdraws consent to the recordings.

segments.title: Consent remains unresolved
segments.body: Wallbridge has not said whether he intends to withdraw consent. He has said he and people close to him believed they were making a feature film and urged TV 2 not to make similar programmes. Pallesen says he is unsure whether the broadcaster would be punished; his assessment is not a court ruling.

content.headline: Manchester United's Chelsea defeat raises relegation fears, but a drop remains a
content.shortHeadline: Chelsea defeat deepens Man Utd's relegation fears
content.standfirst: United's 2-0 loss at Chelsea extended their winless run to nine games in all competitions. Their form has revived talk of a relegation fight, though the gathered analysis says a drop remains unlikely.

image.caption: Chelsea beat Manchester United 2-0 at Stamford Bridge.

sources.originalTitle: Martinez's 'inexplicable' 83 seconds cost Man Utd and Carrick
Are Manchester United really at risk of a relegation scrap?

segments.body: Manchester United lost 2-0 at Chelsea after Lisandro Martinez was sent off in the second half. The defender received a second yellow card and Chelsea then scored again; United have now gone nine matches in all competitions without a win.

segments.title: A worrying position, not a prediction
segments.body: United have seven points from their first nine league games and are 17th. The analysis notes that their current rate would leave them below 30 points over a full season, but says relegation remains unlikely given the club's scale and resources. The club's next steps, including Michael Carrick's future, remain unclear.

perspectives.body: Former World Cup final official Darren Cann called Martinez's actions “inexplicable”, saying the defender made no attempt to play the ball. Carrick said he had not yet seen the incident back.

content.headline: South Africa beat Australia by 176 runs to win Test series 2-1
content.shortHeadline: South Africa rout Australia to win Test series 2-1
content.standfirst: Australia were dismissed for 111 while chasing 288 in Cape Town, giving South Africa a famous final-day victory. Kagiso Rabada struck early and Simon Harmer finished with six wickets.

image.caption: Kagiso Rabada took three wickets early on the final day as South Africa closed in on victory.

sources.originalTitle: 'Un-Australian' - Warner tears into former side after SA charge to win

segments.body: South Africa won the third Test by 176 runs to take the series 2-1. Australia lost two wickets in Kagiso Rabada's first over of the final-day chase and were bowled out for 111, with Simon Harmer taking 6-16.

segments.title: A sharp verdict on Australia's batting
segments.body: Former Australia opener David Warner called his former side's display “terrible” and “utterly disgraceful” on Fox Sports. South Africa's win also lifted them back to the top of the world rankings, according to the report.

content.headline: Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or, ending England's 25-year wait
content.shortHeadline: Kane wins Ballon d'Or and ends England's 25-year wait
content.standfirst: The Bayern Munich and England striker was named the winner after Ronaldo Nazario read out his name. Kane said his heart was beating fast as he waited for the announcement.

sources.originalTitle: 'My heart was beating so fast' - Kane wins Ballon d'Or
German Bundesliga

segments.body: Harry Kane has won the Ballon d'Or, ending England's 25-year wait for a winner, according to BBC Sport. The Bayern Munich striker said his “heart was beating so fast” as Ronaldo Nazario announced the result.

content.headline: De Minaur stuns world number one-bound Zverev in Vienna semi-final
content.shortHeadline: De Minaur beats Zverev in Vienna before Australian faces Alcaraz
content.standfirst: Alex de Minaur recovered from losing the first set to beat Alexander Zverev in three. Zverev will still take the men's world number one ranking on Monday, while De Minaur advances to face Carlos Alcaraz in the final.

image.caption: Alexander Zverev, who lost to Alex de Minaur in Vienna.

sources.originalTitle: World number one-bound Zverev loses to De Minaur

segments.body: Alex de Minaur defeated top seed Alexander Zverev 4-6 6-1 7-6 in the Vienna semi-finals, handing the German his first loss since securing the top ranking. Zverev will replace Jannik Sinner as world number one on Monday.
De Minaur goes on to meet Carlos Alcaraz in the final. The victory also moved the Australian ahead of Rafael Jodar in the race to qualify for the season-ending ATP Finals.

content.headline: Brighton beat Manchester City 1-0 as Verbruggen shines
content.shortHeadline: Verbruggen inspires Brighton to 1-0 win at Man City
content.standfirst: Bart Verbruggen made seven saves as Brighton bounced back from a midweek cup defeat to win at the Etihad. The result leaves Manchester City with successive Premier League losses.

image.caption: Brighton beat Manchester City 1-0 in the Premier League.

sources.originalTitle: Verbruggen spreads belief as Brighton continue to impress
Maresca's big test is to address mounting Man City issues

segments.body: Brighton won 1-0 at Manchester City in the league rematch, three days after losing to them on penalties in the Carabao Cup. Goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen made seven saves, including a second-half stop from Matheus Nunes.

The result was City's second consecutive league defeat. Enzo Maresca said his side had created enough to get more from the game, while Brighton head coach Fabian Hurzeler praised the belief his players showed.

content.headline: Spurs make it three Premier League wins in a row with Palace victory
content.shortHeadline: Spurs beat 10-man Palace for third straight league win
content.standfirst: Tottenham beat Crystal Palace to record three successive Premier League wins for the first time in more than 20 months. Palace played most of the match with 10 men after Jean-Philippe Mateta's early dismissal.

image.caption: Tottenham celebrate their victory over Crystal Palace.

sources.originalTitle: Are De Zerbi's Spurs finding elusive consistency?

segments.body: Tottenham beat Crystal Palace after Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off in the 13th minute. The win extended Spurs' league run to three successive victories, a sequence they had not achieved since February 2025.

Spurs had 34 shots to Palace's two, and moved into the top half of the table. Roberto De Zerbi welcomed his team's focus but said they still needed to improve their finishing and warned that three wins were not enough.

content.headline: Fleetwood knock Arsenal out of the EFL Cup on penalties
content.shortHeadline: Fleetwood stun Arsenal to reach EFL Cup next round
content.standfirst: Fleetwood Town manager Matt Lawlor celebrated after his side eliminated the Premier League champions from the EFL Cup, winning a penalty shootout after a 1-1 draw.

sources.originalTitle: Lawlor delighted after beating 'best team in the country'

segments.body: Fleetwood Town knocked Arsenal out of the EFL Cup on penalties after the teams drew 1-1. Manager Matt Lawlor said he could not hide his delight at the result.

content.headline: Sunderland remain bottom after Coventry defeat as difficult run looms
content.shortHeadline: Sunderland stay bottom after Coventry loss, with tough run ahead
content.standfirst: Sunderland's 3-1 defeat at Coventry left them bottom after nine league games. Their busy European campaign continues, but a demanding run of domestic fixtures makes the league situation increasingly urgent.

image.caption: Coventry beat Sunderland to move out of the bottom three.

sources.originalTitle: Sunderland's paradox - San Siro trip amid relegation battle

segments.body: Sunderland lost 3-1 at Coventry and remained bottom of the Premier League after nine matches. They have six defeats and two draws in the league, while their last league win came on 30 August.

segments.title: A crowded calendar
segments.body: Sunderland have taken seven points from their three Europa League matches, but their league schedule is about to include Chelsea, Aston Villa, Tottenham, Liverpool and Newcastle. Captain Granit Xhaka said the team had made too many mistakes and needed to show character.

content.headline: Morphine’s lost demos capture Mark Sandman before the band’s final album
content.shortHeadline: Morphine’s lost demos capture Mark Sandman’s final sessions
content.standfirst: The newly surfaced recordings reveal a looser side of the band’s work before a fraught label deal sent Mark Sandman back to the studio alone. His partner and bandmates describe the music’s release as a chance to reconnect with him.

image.caption: Mark Sandman performing with Morphine.

sources.originalTitle: ​‘He buckled. I could hear his bass ringing out ...’ The luminous rise and tragic end of US alt heroes Morphine

segments.body: In 1998, Morphine were recording demos for their first album with DreamWorks when pressure to make a hit and disagreement over the sessions strained the band’s relationship with producer Paul Q Kolderie. Mark Sandman left Fort Apache studio and recorded a new set of songs himself; those became the album The Night, released in 2000 after his death.

segments.title: A recording brought back to life
segments.body: Sandman’s partner Sabine Hrechdakian found the earlier demos while sorting through his work. The recordings, now titled Cocoon, preserve a more relaxed sound, with Sandman audible between takes. Dana Colley added saxophone parts for the release, due on 4 December. Hrechdakian describes assembling it as a “healing” experience.

content.headline: The Big Moon turn Juliette Jackson’s hearing loss into hopeful pop
content.shortHeadline: The Big Moon find joy after Juliette Jackson’s hearing loss
content.standfirst: After surgery for a cholesteatoma left the singer with much less hearing on one side, she set aside songs she found too bleak and imagined a happier ending. The result is a bright pop-disco album shaped by that difficult shift.

image.caption: The Big Moon, with Juliette Jackson in red.

sources.originalTitle: The Big Moon: Forever review – the hell of hearing loss inspires a defiantly hopeful pop-disco marvel

segments.body: The Big Moon’s fourth album, Forever, follows a frightening change for frontperson Juliette Jackson: a cholesteatoma diagnosed in 2024 caused her to lose most of her hearing on one side. Because songwriting is both her job and her identity, she says the diagnosis felt existential. Songs she first wrote about the experience were so miserable that she did not want to keep them.

segments.title: Writing toward a brighter ending
segments.body: Jackson instead began imagining the hopeful outcome she wanted, even before she knew whether it would come. That decision gives the album’s danceable songs an extra emotional charge: they celebrate everyday pleasures and the value of being present, while acknowledging illness and the passing of time. The review hears the contrast as convincing rather than forced.

content.headline: Underscores’ April Grey is learning to take pop ambition to bigger stages
content.shortHeadline: Underscores’ April Grey takes her ambitious pop to arenas
content.standfirst: The musician behind U moved from online experimentation to a tightly focused pop record, then found herself playing larger venues and supporting Charli xcx. She talks about the leap in scale—and the love songs she once thought she could not write.

image.caption: Underscores, also known as April Grey.

sources.originalTitle: Pop prodigy Underscores: ‘I don’t think Gen Z is a loveless generation’

segments.body: April Grey, who records as Underscores, says she set out to make U, her third album, feel like a big swing. Released in March, it brought a new wave of listeners to the musician, whose earlier work included the underground successes Fishmonger and Wallsocket. A run of larger headline shows and a support slot on Charli xcx’s tour have made the next challenge figuring out how her show works in an arena.

segments.title: Learning to write about love
segments.body: Grey says the response to the sprawling Wallsocket left her feeling misunderstood, and helped prompt her to try a focused pop album. She set out to write nine love songs, despite finding intimacy difficult and having previously struggled to connect with the genre. She rejects the idea that Gen Z is loveless, while admitting that dating and sex can feel daunting.

content.headline: Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black anniversary revisits the album and its cost
content.shortHeadline: Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black: the songs and the scrutiny
content.standfirst: A journalist recalls an unusually candid meeting with Winehouse as her second album began to take off. A new anniversary edition, meanwhile, revives the music while raising questions about the volume of material and attention that surrounded her.

image.caption: Amy Winehouse during the period when Back to Black was released.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Maybe I should be on Ritalin’: My extraordinary afternoon with Amy Winehouse
Back to Black (20th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: In a first-hand recollection of meeting Amy Winehouse in 2006, journalist Nick Duerden remembers her as funny, open and still surprised by the attention gathering around Back to Black. The album’s songs made a star’s private heartbreak feel immediate, while the singer’s candour drew listeners closer to the person behind them.

segments.title: What an anniversary edition can—and cannot—add
segments.body: A 20th-anniversary edition adds demos, B-sides and a live Amsterdam performance to an album that Pitchfork calls one of the great breakup records. The review argues that the new material is limited and that the reissue cannot fill the larger absence left by Winehouse’s small catalogue. It also stresses how relentless public scrutiny amplified the pressure around a difficult period in her life.

perspectives.body: Pitchfork’s review treats the anniversary package as a reminder of the limits of archival releases: even new demos and live recordings cannot supply the lost follow-up or replace the original album’s particular force.

content.headline: Taylor Swift’s MySpace fans remember the singer before fame
content.shortHeadline: Taylor Swift’s MySpace years, remembered by an early fan
content.standfirst: As Swift’s debut album turns 20, a former teenage fan looks back at discovering the young country singer online and building a sense of community around her songs. The essay traces how that intimacy helped make the artist’s early success feel shared.

image.caption: Taylor Swift as a teenage country singer.

sources.originalTitle: The Taylor Swift I knew on MySpace in 2006

segments.body: Before Taylor Swift became a global star, a teenage fan in Leicester followed her on MySpace, trading news and building friendships with other listeners. The writer remembers Swift’s self-written songs and carefully shared details of her life as making her feel like a peer, not a distant celebrity.

segments.title: A fan community grows with the artist
segments.body: Swift’s debut, released in October 2006, gave the writer and friends songs to put on their profiles and lyrics to treat as personal messages. Looking back, the essay sees the online bond as part of the experience of growing up with Swift’s career: fans felt they were participating in her rise, even as she became increasingly famous and remote from that early image.

content.headline: Manic Street Preachers revisit The Holy Bible and Richey Edwards’ absence
content.shortHeadline: The Manics revisit The Holy Bible and Richey Edwards’ absence
content.standfirst: James Dean Bradfield reflects on performing the band’s stark 1994 album and the new live release drawn from its anniversary shows. He describes how its words still weigh on the group, whose work continues to carry the absence of lyricist Richey Edwards.

image.caption: Nicky Wire, James Dean Bradfield and Sean Moore of Manic Street Preachers.

sources.originalTitle: Manic Street Preachers: ‘We just weren’t equipped to deal with Richey’s problems’

segments.body: The Holy Bible Live documents Manic Street Preachers playing their 1994 album in full at London’s Roundhouse in 2014. Frontman James Dean Bradfield says taking the record back on stage was a physical and emotional challenge: its lyrics still feel heavy, particularly in songs shaped by Richey Edwards’ intense and often disturbing writing.

segments.title: A record the band still carries
segments.body: Edwards disappeared in 1995 and was legally declared dead in 2008. Bradfield says the band were young and ill-equipped to respond to Edwards’ serious mental-health struggles, even though they tried to help. He rejects the idea of easy closure, but says the anniversary performances let the remaining members connect again with the work—and felt like doing it justice.

content.headline: Aphex Twin’s Drukqs bridges rave invention and concert-hall precision
content.shortHeadline: Aphex Twin’s Drukqs: a sprawling meeting of rave and avant-garde
content.standfirst: A 25th-anniversary edition puts the 100-minute album back in focus. Pitchfork hears Richard D James testing the limits between club rhythms and prepared piano, dance music and experimental composition—and turning the album’s sprawl into part of its meaning.

sources.originalTitle: Drukqs (25th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: Released in 2001, Aphex Twin’s Drukqs stretched across two discs and 30 tracks, moving between fast, intricately programmed beats and compositions for a digitally controlled, sometimes prepared piano. Pitchfork’s anniversary review argues that the album brought the club and conservatory traditions into unusually close contact, without smoothing away their differences.

segments.title: An album that pushes at its limits
segments.body: The review follows the music as it blurs rhythm into pitch, acoustic instruments into electronic ones, and dancefloor energy into more abstract forms. Its length and abrupt shifts can feel challenging, but the critic sees that apparent incoherence as central to the record: the album repeatedly strains against musical boundaries and its own capacity.

content.headline: Eris Drew and Octo Octa turn dance-music history into Alchemical Sisters
content.shortHeadline: Eris Drew and Octo Octa make a maximalist dance-music collage
content.standfirst: The New Hampshire-based partners built their first joint full-length from synths, psych-folk instruments and samples from their dance-music archive. Pitchfork hears a warm, oversized tribute to 1990s big beat, with a more intimate highlight in “Song for New Hampshire”.

sources.originalTitle: Alchemical Sisters

segments.body: For Alchemical Sisters, Eris Drew and Octo Octa transformed a bedroom in their New Hampshire cabin into a studio and drew on years of collected dance records. The resulting album combines synths and psych-folk instruments with a maximalist sound that recalls the scale and exuberance of 1990s big beat.

segments.title: A shared history, and a quieter centre
segments.body: The review hears the duo folding older dance sounds into new productions, often making it difficult to tell where a sample ends and their own playing begins. Its standout is “Song for New Hampshire”, a warm, personal track that steps away from the album’s more referential rush and reflects the artists’ life together.

content.headline: Manhood examines the booming business of penile enhancement
content.shortHeadline: Manhood examines the business of penile enhancement
content.standfirst: Daniel Lombroso’s documentary follows a practitioner and men seeking procedures, connecting body-image pressures to loneliness and masculinity. Its subjects include a father whose pursuit of enhancement puts his family under strain.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Never big enough’: inside the booming penis enlargement industry

segments.body: In the documentary Manhood, filmmaker Daniel Lombroso follows Bill Moore, a businessman selling penile-enhancement procedures from a Dallas office, and the men who seek them. Moore presents the procedures as a way to improve confidence and relationships; the film also highlights the risks and the blurred line between cosmetic treatment and medical care.

segments.title: More than a question of size
segments.body: The film’s stories connect the demand for enhancement to ideas about masculinity, social status and loneliness. One customer, Ruben, wants a procedure badly enough to move his family in with an ex to raise money for it, leaving his wife distressed. Lombroso says he wanted to explore these contradictions without dictating how viewers should respond.

content.headline: Ten unsettling films that find terror beyond the horror genre
content.shortHeadline: Ten films that terrify without being horror movies
content.standfirst: For Halloween, Guardian writers pick films whose dread comes from human cruelty, social pressure or the fear of losing control. Their choices range from Burning and The Hunchback of Notre Dame to 2001: A Space Odyssey and How to Have Sex.

image.caption: Mia McKenna-Bruce in How to Have Sex.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I left shellshocked’: writers on their scariest non-horror movies

segments.body: The Guardian’s Halloween selection looks beyond conventional horror for films that leave viewers shaken. Burning turns an unexplained disappearance into a study of dread and male anger; The Hunchback of Notre Dame is remembered for its depiction of public cruelty; and 2001: A Space Odyssey makes technological progress feel frightening as well as wondrous.

segments.title: Everyday fears, made cinematic
segments.body: Other writers choose How to Have Sex for its sustained sense of vulnerability, The Hunt for the way a false accusation turns a community against one of its own, and Dark Waters for the scale of a corporation’s indifference. The selections show how fear can come from recognisable institutions and relationships, not just monsters or jump scares.

content.headline: Fourteen box-office flops that deserve another look
content.shortHeadline: Fourteen film flops worth rediscovering
content.standfirst: A new box-office disaster can still become a favourite later. This selection makes the case for ambitious films whose commercial failures obscured their pleasures, from The Thing and Dune to Cloud Atlas and Babylon.

sources.originalTitle: The 14 spectacular film flops that are actually worth watching

segments.body: The list argues that a poor box-office showing is not the same as a poor film. Its examples range from John Carpenter’s The Thing, initially crowded out by more upbeat releases, to David Lynch’s strange, much-criticised adaptation of Dune and the Coen brothers’ screwball comedy The Hudsucker Proxy.

segments.title: Missed on release, reconsidered later
segments.body: Other picks include the self-aware action comedy Last Action Hero, the ambitious science-fiction film Cloud Atlas and Damien Chazelle’s Hollywood epic Babylon. The reasons for their commercial struggles vary, but the list’s invitation is consistent: look past opening-weekend results and decide what these films offer on their own terms.

content.headline: November film picks: from Elsinore to a new Hunger Games prequel
content.shortHeadline: November’s films: Elsinore, The Hunger Games and more
content.standfirst: The month’s cinema and streaming choices include Andrew Scott as Hamlet actor Ian Charleson, a new Hunger Games prequel and an account of disability-rights activist Judith Heumann. The guide also flags the comedy Club Kid and political drama Wild Horse Nine.

sources.originalTitle: Elsinore to The Hunger Games: 12 of the best films to watch in November

segments.body: Among November’s releases, Elsinore tells the story of Ian Charleson taking over Hamlet after Daniel Day-Lewis left the production, with Andrew Scott playing Charleson and Olivia Colman his doctor. The guide also highlights Being Heumann, about US disability-rights activist Judith Heumann and the 1977 occupation of San Francisco’s federal building by campaigners demanding equal rights.

segments.title: New worlds and returning stories
segments.body: For franchise fans, Sunrise on the Reaping returns to Panem decades before Katniss Everdeen’s story, while Club Kid follows a New York party promoter who meets the son he never knew he had. The guide also points to Wild Horse Nine, Martin McDonagh’s story of two CIA agents on Easter Island, and several other releases across the month.

content.headline: Yaga mixes Slavic folklore, detective work and debauched folk horror
content.shortHeadline: Yaga turns a missing-person case into comic folk horror
content.standfirst: A detective searching for a missing heir finds cult activity and hints of the Slavic witch Baba Yaga in a small fishing town. The review enjoys the series’ irreverent mix of mystery, sex and supernatural menace, while wondering how long it will keep the witch at a distance.

image.caption: Carrie-Anne Moss as Katherine in Yaga.

sources.originalTitle: Yaga: chicken bones? Saltburn parties? This folk horror is so debauched, it’s hilarious

segments.body: In Yaga, detective Charlie Rapp arrives in the fishing town of Whittock to investigate the disappearance of Henry Park, a wealthy family’s son. The case grows violent and points towards a cult and a supernatural presence. The series draws on Slavic folklore about Baba Yaga, whose taunting voice opens and closes each episode.

segments.title: A witch, or an idea?
segments.body: The review praises the series’ playful mix of mismatched detectives, masked parties, sex and horror imagery, along with its formidable women characters. It remains unclear, several episodes in, whether Baba Yaga is a literal figure or a symbol of women’s anger at men. The critic likes the ambiguity but hopes the show will eventually deliver an actual witch.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors finale delivers a Faithful win after a shaky series
content.shortHeadline: The Celebrity Traitors ends with a surprise Faithful victory
content.standfirst: Bash spots the danger in Kenny’s decision to end the game and persuades Romesh Ranganathan to change his vote, securing the Faithfuls’ win. Critics differ on whether the finale rescued a series whose recruitment twists and early blunders had weakened its momentum.

image.caption: The Celebrity Traitors contestants at the Endgame Round Table.

sources.originalTitle: One player’s lack of ego saved Celebrity Traitors
Sky-high ratings – for a lacklustre series: The Celebrity Traitors has become too nice for its own good
James Acaster was stitched up

segments.body: The Celebrity Traitors finale turned on Bash noticing that Kenny’s choice to end the game with several players still at the table looked suspicious. After a tied vote, Bash persuaded Romesh Ranganathan to change his mind; Kenny was banished, giving the Faithfuls the victory and £83,000 for their chosen charities. The i Paper argues that Bash’s lack of ego helped him see what others missed.

segments.title: Was the season saved?
segments.body: The finale’s surprise contrasts with a season that critics found uneven. The Guardian says frequent recruitments and a cast wary of conflict undermined suspense. The i Paper’s account of the season’s early mechanics points to Richard E Grant’s accidental confession and James Acaster’s unwanted recruitment as problems that put pressure on the game well before the finale.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s critique argues that the series became too polite and that repeated recruitments made it harder for the Faithful to sustain theories or for the story to build momentum.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after its Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future after Disney+ deal ends
content.standfirst: With the planned Christmas special cancelled, no new Doctor announced and the BBC seeking a funding partner, the long-running series is at a pause. Fans and writers disagree about what went wrong, but hope the show’s history of reinvention will carry it forward.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+ on Doctor Who, and a planned Christmas special has been cancelled. The corporation is looking for a new partner to help finance future episodes, but has not announced a new Doctor or given more detail. The pause follows the departure of Ncuti Gatwa after the 2025 series.

segments.title: A show built on change
segments.body: The article traces the series’ history of reinvention, from its 1989 cancellation to Russell T Davies’s successful 2005 revival and later changes of lead actor and showrunner. Fans quoted in the piece differ over the latest era: some point to confusing scripts and a lack of focus, while others object to the long wait and the loss of the show’s international funding deal. Its next chapter remains unsettled.

content.headline: 70 Up ends a six-decade experiment—and revisits its participants’ doubts
content.shortHeadline: 70 Up closes a six-decade portrait of lives and class
content.standfirst: The final instalment of ITV’s long-running series catches up with its surviving participants and looks again at how the project portrayed them. Some contributors value the opportunity; others say the edit reduced complex lives to a version they did not recognise.

image.caption: The contributors to the Up documentary series as children.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A little pill of poison’: Why the cast of 70 Up came to resent it

segments.body: ITV’s Seven Up! began in 1964 by following 14 children from different backgrounds and asking what their lives might become. The final programme, 70 Up, returns to the surviving participants and ends a documentary project that revisited them every seven years. Asif Kapadia took over directing after Michael Apted’s death in 2021.

segments.title: The limits of a life on screen
segments.body: The article considers the project’s influence alongside the participants’ unease about its framing. Peter Davies left for years after tabloids attacked his remarks about Margaret Thatcher, and says there was always more to him than the version shown. Another participant criticised the programme’s assumptions about women and men. The series producer says trust remained, while acknowledging that years of life must be compressed into brief films.

content.headline: Night Plane turns a flight-attendant job simulator into an indie horror trip
content.shortHeadline: Night Plane turns a flight-attendant sim into horror
content.standfirst: What begins as routine airport work becomes a strange loop of check-ins, demons and a crashed plane. The review finds the low-poly game funny and unsettling in equal measure, with enough hidden quests and endings to reward a return trip.

image.caption: A scene from the low-poly horror game Night Plane.

sources.originalTitle: Night Plane review – join the jumbo jet to hell in this indie horror head trip

segments.body: Night Plane casts the player as a flight attendant handling check-ins and serving passengers before a crash sends the game into an uncanny cycle. Back at the airport, some passengers may be demons in disguise. Its deliberately rough, low-poly graphics recall the original PlayStation era and make the strange encounters harder to read.

segments.title: A joke with a disturbing edge
segments.body: The game’s humour initially suggests a horror spoof, but flickering cabin lights, disjointed dialogue and images of wreckage make its nightmare increasingly unsettling. The review praises the shift between laughs and scares, and says that a four-to-five-hour first playthrough leaves further quests and endings to discover.

content.headline: AI-assisted game mashups raise new questions about copyright and piracy
content.shortHeadline: AI game mashups bring modding and copyright into sharper focus
content.standfirst: Tools that can help reconstruct and alter game code have made elaborate fan mashups faster to build. The Guardian’s games writer tests how accessible the process has become and considers the consequences for publishers and creators.

image.caption: A video-game mashup shown in a social-media clip.

sources.originalTitle: Social media is full of weird video game mashups. Where are they all coming from?

segments.body: Clips of unlikely game mashups have spread across social media, from Skyrim in Minecraft to Mario appearing in Halo. The Guardian’s games writer traces much of the trend to AI-assisted decompilation: software that can help turn a compiled game back into editable source code, lowering the time and technical expertise needed to modify it.

segments.title: A new scale of risk
segments.body: The writer says a simple browser game was quick to produce with an AI tool, though the result was crude and still required human input. The bigger concern is the ease of distributing code, emulators and game libraries, with potential implications for copyright and piracy. The article asks whether AI companies will face stronger limits now that these tools can affect major publishers as well as individual creators.

content.headline: Eight indie horror games to try this Halloween
content.shortHeadline: Eight new indie horror games for Halloween
content.standfirst: This season’s independent releases include a dark fairy-tale adventure, a card game against the devil and a short horror set in a Scottish takeaway. The selection also points to Silver Pines and Tenebris Somnia for players seeking puzzles and eerie atmosphere.

image.caption: A scene from The Killing Stone, an occult card game.

sources.originalTitle: Eight great new indie horror games for Halloween

segments.body: The Guardian’s Halloween guide surveys eight indie horror releases. Allogloom turns a search for a missing mother into a surreal, picture-book adventure, while The Killing Stone casts a card game against the devil as a way to win back a lost soul. Silver Pines pairs a missing-person case with puzzles in an abandoned town, and Tenebris Somnia blends pixel art with live-action sequences.

segments.title: From unsettling to outrageous
segments.body: Other picks range from a Scottish takeaway serving a mysterious dish to a game about a woman fleeing a 17th-century witch-hunt. The list also includes Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival and a story about a penguin observing Lovecraftian horrors in Antarctica. The selection favours different kinds of scares, from atmospheric adventure to gore and dark comedy.

content.headline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans mourning a role-playing giant
content.shortHeadline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans mourning
content.standfirst: EA’s decision to close the studio cancels its forthcoming Mass Effect game and puts hundreds of jobs at risk. A longtime fan and games-industry worker explains what BioWare’s character-driven role-playing games meant to players.

image.caption: A scene from Mass Effect 3.

sources.originalTitle: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft

segments.body: EA has announced BioWare’s closure, cancelling its forthcoming Mass Effect game and putting more than 400 jobs at stake, according to the article. The studio made influential role-playing games including Mass Effect, Dragon Age and Knights of the Old Republic. The writer, who has worked in the games industry for 15 years, describes the news as the end of a studio that shaped a generation of players.

segments.title: A story shaped by the player
segments.body: The writer recalls how the Mass Effect trilogy’s squadmates and consequential choices made the story feel personal: decisions could affect relationships, characters and the wider galaxy across three games. BioWare’s recent struggles are acknowledged, but the cancellation of another instalment still leaves fans wondering what the series might have become in the right hands.

content.headline: Replaying Modern Warfare 2 helps a father and son find their rhythm
content.shortHeadline: A father and son reconnect through Modern Warfare 2
content.standfirst: The writer and his 22-year-old son return to co-op missions they first tried when the son was five. Their repeated failures become a source of laughter, teamwork and an unexpectedly moving shared memory.

image.caption: A scene from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game the pair revisit.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: A father and his adult son revisit the Special Ops missions in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the first game they played together in 2009. The son now charges ahead while his father plays cautiously; at first, those different instincts mean they keep failing the same challenges they could not beat years ago.

segments.title: Learning to play together again
segments.body: Gradually, they find a balance: one moves in close while the other covers him from a distance. Completing the missions brings the father back to the uncomplicated pleasure of gaming with his child. Their time together is temporary—the pair expect to move to different parts of the world in a few months—but his son says he will remember these weeks as some of their best times.

content.headline: Does a video-game romance count as cheating? GTA VI sparks debate
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s virtual romance raises real-world relationship questions
content.standfirst: Social-media users argue that caring for Grand Theft Auto VI’s couple amounts to infidelity. The debate, the writer suggests, reflects different relationship boundaries—and anxieties about feeling less valued than a virtual partner.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason, the couple at the centre of Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: A look at Grand Theft Auto VI prompted an unexpected argument online: whether players who build a relationship between protagonists Lucia and Jason are being unfaithful. The game’s interactions include dates, messages and other ways to strengthen the couple’s bond. Some social-media users say those actions cross a line; others see them as ordinary role-playing.

segments.title: A debate about attention
segments.body: The writer rejects the blanket claim that in-game romance is cheating, while noting that partners can set different boundaries. The essay argues that the controversy also points to a real concern: someone may feel hurt if their partner lavishes attention on a fictional character while neglecting them. In a wider climate of loneliness and strained dating, the game has become a screen for anxieties that exist beyond it.

content.headline: Light-guided nerve therapy shows early promise for restoring sight
content.shortHeadline: Light-guided gene therapy partly restores sight in early trial
content.standfirst: In a small study, six of 10 people with severe vision loss from retinitis pigmentosa gained useful sight in one treated eye. The approach remains experimental, while researchers explore other possible uses for optogenetics.

image.caption: Light can be used to activate nerve cells with precision.

sources.originalTitle: A cure for blindness is coming

segments.body: The treatment uses gene therapy to make nerve cells in the retina respond to amber light. Patients wear special glasses that convert ordinary light into amber shades, prompting the cells to fire. It does not restore normal vision: participants first perceived dots of light and had to learn to interpret them.

segments.title: A research tool becoming a treatment
segments.body: In the study, published in The New England Journal of Medicine, six of 10 treated patients showed meaningful improvement after three months; they could do tasks such as picking up a cup, but could not distinguish faces. The results are an early sign of potential, not evidence of a cure.

Researchers are also investigating optogenetics for pain, epilepsy and hearing. Those applications are at earlier stages: some are still being tested in animals, and the approach can require gene therapy. Researchers say safety must be established, particularly where a treatment may be irreversible.

content.headline: Tiny magnetic robots could deliver drugs precisely inside the body
content.shortHeadline: Micro-robots offer a new route to targeted drug delivery
content.standfirst: Researchers are testing devices that can be steered through the gut and, in animal experiments, the bloodstream. The work is promising, but most of these technologies remain far from routine patient use.

image.caption: Illustration of a small robot designed to deliver medicine inside the gut.

sources.originalTitle: The astonishing micro-robots you swallow that spot cancer and might help treat it

segments.body: A 6.5mm magnetic robot developed by researchers in Beijing was used to deliver insulin to the lower intestine of pigs, according to a study published this month in Cyborg and Bionic Systems. Its spikes help it attach to gut tissue and release its drug payload. The result is an animal test, not a demonstrated treatment in people.

segments.title: From cameras to experimental treatments
segments.body: Magnetic steering is already used to guide some swallowable camera capsules around the stomach during examinations. More ambitious devices are being developed to deliver drugs to specific sites, with the aim of limiting the amount released elsewhere in the body. Researchers have proposed potential uses including tumours and blood clots, but these applications are at different stages of development.

A separate team has guided a 2mm robot through a pig’s bloodstream under imaging, while other researchers are developing swarms of much smaller magnetic particles. Some possible applications have only been demonstrated in models or mice. Devices small enough to travel through human blood vessels and treat patients are still years away, according to the report.

content.headline: Fifty years on, The Selfish Gene remains influential—and contested
content.shortHeadline: The Selfish Gene at 50: influential, flawed and still debated
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s editorial reflects on why Richard Dawkins’ book became a landmark of popular science, while noting that evolutionary biology has moved on and that its argument has long drawn criticism.

image.caption: Richard Dawkins’ book has remained a touchstone—and a source of debate—for half a century.

sources.originalTitle: The Guardian view on 50 years of The Selfish Gene: flawed, outdated, yet still a model of truly popular science writing

segments.body: First published in 1976, The Selfish Gene sold millions and became a widely read account of evolution. The Guardian’s editorial argues that its force came partly from a provocative central idea: complex behaviour, including altruism, could be explained through the competition and persistence of genes.

perspectives.body: The editorial praises the book’s vivid, argumentative style as a model for popular science writing, while stressing that its scientific claims and polemical framing remain open to criticism.

segments.title: The argument and its critics
segments.body: The editorial notes that biologists have disputed whether genes should be treated as the primary focus of natural selection and criticises the book’s tendency to explain traits as adaptations. It says evolutionary biology recognises a larger role for chance and randomness, and that the book concentrates overwhelmingly on animals.

content.headline: UK regulator outlines ways platforms could check users’ ages
content.shortHeadline: Ofcom sets out possible age checks for social media
content.standfirst: Photo ID, banking checks, facial age estimation and digital ID are among Ofcom’s suggested methods ahead of a planned UK ban on social media for under-16s. Government approval is still pending, and no check can eliminate circumvention.

sources.originalTitle: Ofcom outlines age check methods ahead of social media ban for under-16s

segments.body: Ofcom has identified four methods it considers highly effective for assessing whether someone is at least 16: matching photo ID to a live image, checking age through a bank, estimating age from a face, and using digital ID. The regulator says platforms must preserve privacy and protect personal data, but leaves them to decide how to implement checks.

segments.title: How the checks would work
segments.body: The proposed UK restrictions are due to take effect in March next year and cover major services including Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat. Many adults may also have to demonstrate that they are old enough to use the platforms. Ofcom says it does not yet know how many accounts would need to be checked.

segments.title: Questions about enforcement
segments.body: The guidance still needs government approval, and Ofcom acknowledges that some children may get around age checks. Child-safety organisations welcomed the proposals but pointed to difficulties in enforcing Australia’s comparable ban. The Molly Rose Foundation also questioned Ofcom’s record of enforcing the Online Safety Act.

content.headline: The dark web is not as distant from everyday data theft as it seems
content.shortHeadline: Stolen data links everyday users to the dark web
content.standfirst: A CNET investigation traces how personal information moves through breaches, criminal forums and marketplaces—and why avoiding the dark web does not keep a person’s data out of criminal hands.

image.caption: Diagram illustrating how Tor routes traffic through layers of encryption.

sources.originalTitle: The Dark Web Is Hiding in Plain Sight. Chances Are It’s Got Your Data

segments.body: The dark web is a part of the internet accessed through networks such as Tor, which can make it harder to identify users and servers. Tor also has legitimate privacy uses, including for readers and sources who want to communicate with news organisations more privately. It is not the same as the “deep web”, which includes ordinary private accounts and inboxes that search engines do not index.

segments.title: How stolen information circulates
segments.body: The report describes stolen credentials and personal records being traded across criminal marketplaces, forums and encrypted channels. Some information is used for fraud or to break into accounts; other data becomes leverage in extortion attacks. Marketplaces are not necessarily confined to Tor: the report notes that some criminal services have operated on the ordinary web as well.

segments.title: Steps that can limit exposure
segments.body: Services such as Have I Been Pwned can show whether an email address appears in known breaches, but a clean result cannot prove that information was never exposed. The report advises changing reused or exposed passwords, using unique passwords and multifactor authentication, and considering a credit freeze if identity fraud is a concern. These steps make data harder to exploit; they cannot retrieve copies already stolen.

content.headline: TikTok’s restaurant guide is part of a wider push to become a super app
content.shortHeadline: TikTok expands from videos into bookings, shopping and payments
content.standfirst: A restaurant guide joins a growing set of TikTok services for discovery, shopping and travel. The company’s expansion could keep more activity inside the app, though some proposed payment features remain in development.

sources.originalTitle: From restaurant guides to payments, here’s how TikTok is building a super app

segments.body: TikTok’s Must Eat restaurant guide draws on more than 40 million posts and comments, letting users browse recommendations by city, cuisine, price, rating and location. The launch adds a more structured search tool to a platform where restaurant videos already influence where people choose to eat.

segments.title: Building an all-in-one platform
segments.body: The guide fits a broader expansion that includes TikTok Shop, travel bookings, games, sports features and more detailed local search. TikTok has also been reported to be developing money transfers through direct messages; that feature is not described as launched. The aim is to help users discover and complete more activities without leaving the app.

The strategy brings TikTok into closer competition with services such as Google Maps, Yelp and online marketplaces. The report compares the ambition with the super-app model popular in China, while noting that it is uncertain whether a similar approach will work as well elsewhere.

content.headline: AI demand is squeezing PC components as Intel warns of a weaker quarter
content.shortHeadline: Intel flags PC pressure as AI demand strains component supply
content.standfirst: Intel’s shares plunged after it forecast lower-than-expected fourth-quarter revenue and said rising memory prices were weighing on PC demand. Its data-centre business grew, but the company faces constraints on expanding chip production.

sources.originalTitle: Intel’s stock crashes, knocking $12B from government’s stake

segments.body: Intel shares fell about 28% after the company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $15bn to $16bn, below analysts’ expectations, and warned its gross margin would fall. Chief executive Lip-Bu Tan said higher memory prices and reduced availability were pushing up computer prices and adding pressure to already limited IT budgets.

segments.title: A different picture in data centres
segments.body: Intel reported that revenue from its data-centre business rose 78% from a year earlier. But it said growth is constrained by available capacity at its factories and the need to attract more external customers. One new Arizona factory is operating; another is not expected to come online until 2028.

content.headline: Northumberland awaits proposed tests for new data-centre projects
content.shortHeadline: Northumberland data centres face proposed local-benefit tests
content.standfirst: The UK government says new centres should support local communities, create jobs and protect water supplies. In Northumberland, where one large project has approval and two more are under consideration, local representatives say the details will matter.

image.caption: A data-centre development is planned at Cambois, Northumberland.

sources.originalTitle: New data centres must bring 'local benefits'

segments.body: Chancellor John Healey has said data centres should face “strict tests” requiring investment in local communities, local jobs and protection for water supplies. If companies meet the conditions, they would receive the grid connections they need and could, where necessary, build temporary on-site power generation.

segments.title: A live local test
