segments.body: Northumberland County Council has approved a £10bn data-centre project by US company QTS at Cambois and is considering two further applications. The council’s Conservative leader called development important for the economy if handled carefully; Labour MP Ian Lavery welcomed the government’s pledge but said its detail was crucial.

Lavery has raised concerns that several centres concentrated in a small area could occupy industrial land that might support businesses with more local jobs. He also said officials should listen more closely to residents. The report does not set out the final tests or how they would be enforced.

content.headline: Investor caution puts pressure on the AI infrastructure spending boom
content.shortHeadline: AI spending boom faces tougher questions from investors
content.standfirst: Big technology companies are spending heavily on AI infrastructure as cash flow weakens and investors reassess returns. Reports of financing challenges and a proposed Nvidia loan guarantee show how the buildout may depend on capital beyond companies’ operating profits.

sources.originalTitle: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom
Nvidia weighs playing the cosigner for Nscale’s AI data center in West Virginia
OpenAI reportedly lowers funding target for new round

segments.body: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft have outlined more than $740bn in capital spending for the year, much of it linked to AI infrastructure, according to TechCrunch. The report says investors are increasingly focused on negative free cash flow, debt and whether the investments will generate sufficient returns.

segments.title: More than one way to fund the buildout
segments.body: The report describes negative free cash flow at Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, while Microsoft remained cash-flow positive in its latest quarter. It also cites $326bn in debt raised in 2026 by Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle. Strong demand for cloud computing continues, but the costs of meeting it are becoming a growing concern for investors.

Separately, TechCrunch reports that Nvidia is in talks to guarantee construction financing for an AI data-centre project planned by Nscale for Anthropic. The proposed arrangement would make Nvidia responsible if Nscale defaulted, subject to the terms reported. TechCrunch also reports that OpenAI’s latest fundraising target has reportedly been reduced to $20bn from an earlier $30bn, with $11bn secured so far, according to the Wall Street Journal. These are reported negotiations and funding figures, not evidence that the projects or financing plans have been completed.

perspectives.body: The Nscale report highlights a specific financing mechanism: Nvidia could guarantee construction debt, deepening its financial ties to a provider building capacity for a major customer.

content.headline: Anthropic’s IPO filing sets out AI’s promises—and its risks
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic’s IPO filing pairs AI ambitions with stark risks
content.standfirst: The company’s lengthy stock-market prospectus presents advanced AI as a source of discovery and potential danger, while disclosing large financial commitments and a risk of continued losses. A separate credit-rating forecast adds uncertainty, not a settled assessment.

sources.originalTitle: Silicon Valley wants you to invest in miracles
Anthropic expected to receive high ‘junk’ rating from credit agencies following IPO, FT report says

segments.body: Anthropic’s 335-page S-1 filing describes its ambitions for advanced AI in expansive terms, but also warns that systems developed without appropriate safeguards could pose catastrophic or existential risks. The Verge reports that the document includes 94 pages of risk factors and frames the company’s public-benefit status as part of its effort to balance social aims with shareholder interests.

segments.title: The financial questions
segments.body: The filing, as described in the report, discloses large commitments to secure computing capacity and plans to build data-centre infrastructure, while warning that Anthropic may not become profitable. The article notes that third-quarter results were absent, leaving investors without information that could help assess the company’s costs and profitability.

TechCrunch reports that Blackstone told investors it expects Anthropic could receive a double-B credit rating after its IPO, a speculative-grade rating that could make borrowing more expensive. That is Blackstone’s forecast, not a rating already issued by a credit agency; Anthropic and Blackstone declined to comment to TechCrunch.

content.headline: Major AI companies back a shared signal for websites to limit scraping
content.shortHeadline: AI firms back a shared website signal to limit scraping
content.standfirst: A proposed standard would let publishers express AI-training preferences through a shared setting in robots.txt, rather than configuring rules company by company. Major firms say they will adopt it, but Meta has not said whether it will honour the signal.

sources.originalTitle: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping

segments.body: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic say they will adopt a shared “policy token” that publishers could place in a website’s robots.txt file to communicate whether AI crawlers may access content. The proposal is being developed through the Internet Engineering Task Force, according to The Verge.

segments.title: A common signal, not a licensing deal
segments.body: The proposed setting aims to let publishers state preferences across multiple AI companies instead of configuring each crawler separately. The companies say their crawlers will respect the token. Microsoft says publishers could also distinguish between use for AI training and AI grounding; its report says websites would still appear in Bing search results.

The standard does not itself settle disputes over permission, payment or existing use of content. Anthropic has adopted the signal, while Google and Microsoft plan to support it next year and OpenAI says implementation is planned in the coming months. Meta expressed support for a common signal but did not commit to honouring it.

content.headline: Australian critics say a proposed AI copyright change could trigger a legal test
content.shortHeadline: Proposed AI copyright changes raise Australian legal concerns
content.standfirst: Critics argue that allowing AI firms to scrape copyrighted material could raise constitutional questions about acquiring property without fair compensation. No legislation has been proposed, and the legal outcome would depend on its wording.

image.caption: Australia’s attorney general, Michelle Rowland, says future copyright changes should provide meaningful control and fair compensation.

sources.originalTitle: Experts warn AI copyright changes could breach Australian constitution and spark huge compensation rights case

segments.body: Australian senators and representatives of the recording industry have warned that weakening copyright rules to let AI companies use online material could prompt a constitutional challenge. The concern centres on a provision allowing the Commonwealth to acquire property only on “just terms”.

segments.title: An unresolved legal question
segments.body: Constitutional law expert Anne Twomey said the issue was complex and that the potential concern would depend on how any law was drafted. She noted that no legislative proposal had yet been published. The attorney general’s department said it was alert to the issue, while the government says future copyright changes should provide meaningful control and fair compensation.

AI companies have argued that existing licensing arrangements can be difficult and have promoted an opt-out approach. Creators and industry representatives say current copyright rules should be used instead, and warn that any Australian change could affect international rights holders too. The gather does not establish whether the government will adopt a proposal or how a court would rule.

content.headline: Pope Leo urges international limits on autonomous weapons
content.shortHeadline: Pope Leo calls for steps to ban lethal autonomous weapons
content.standfirst: In an address ahead of a UN meeting in Geneva, the pope said decisions involving human life and force must remain under responsible human oversight. He urged member states to take concrete steps towards banning lethal autonomous weapons.

sources.originalTitle: Pope Leo calls for the disarmament of AI: ‘Machines are tools, not persons’

segments.body: Pope Leo XIV called on UN member states to take concrete steps towards banning lethal autonomous weapons during a meeting in Geneva next month. He said AI systems should be “disarmed” and that people have a responsibility to guide, change or reject how the technology is used.

segments.title: Human oversight
segments.body: The address argues that decisions affecting human life, freedom and the use of force must remain subject to informed human oversight. The pope also cautioned against treating AI systems as persons with rights or legal status, and called for shared standards, independent oversight and accountability.

content.headline: AI-enabled impersonation put a journalist’s byline on fabricated work
content.shortHeadline: A suspected AI scammer used a journalist’s name and byline
content.standfirst: A fake writer pitched editors using the identity and published work of journalist Caroline Williams; Science published an article under her name before the deception was discovered. The person who submitted it disputes that they impersonated her.

sources.originalTitle: My identity was stolen by an AI scammer. It could happen to anyone

segments.body: Editors at several publications received pitches from someone claiming to be Caroline Williams, a UK freelance journalist. Science published a feature under her name and paid the writer $1,000; after the impersonation was uncovered, the journal removed the article. Science said its software indicated the first draft had been written with AI and that it contained quotes copied from other online articles.

segments.title: A disputed account
segments.body: The person who submitted the article told The i Paper they were a different journalist with the same name and had not intended to present Williams’s work as their own. They said linking to her earlier article in a pitch was a mistake. Science’s managing news editor said the person had clearly identified themselves as the UK journalist.

Science has since changed its policies so editors will speak with new writers by phone or video call and use AI-detection software. Williams said the episode threatened her reputation with editors and scientists. The report also notes that AI detection was presented as the journal’s assessment, not independent proof of authorship.

content.headline: A hands-on AI pendant shows the promise—and limits—of build-it-yourself gadgets
content.shortHeadline: An AI pendant’s promise depends on code—and cloud services
content.standfirst: A Verge reporter adapted an inexpensive development kit into a customizable AI companion with help from a coding assistant. The DIY project exposed practical limits, including dependence on Meta’s servers and unanswered questions about the planned commercial device.

sources.originalTitle: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could

segments.body: The Verge’s reporter bought a $50 Waveshare touchscreen pendant and connected it to Meta’s Muse AI service. The device initially offered limited replies and little useful functionality; the reporter used Claude Code to add features such as spoken answers, a conversation history, a camera viewfinder and a virtual-pet game.

segments.title: A prototype with trade-offs
segments.body: The author says they have no coding experience and cannot vouch for the quality or safety of the code. They kept the device on guest Wi-Fi and did not trust it with email or a home network. The pendant’s responsiveness also depended on Meta’s servers, which sometimes lagged.

The experience raises a question the review cannot resolve: whether Meta’s planned Muse Charm will be as freely programmable as a development kit, or offer enough independent value to justify another device. The author found the gadget’s strongest case was its customizability, not the AI assistant alone.
